learning_goal: Classify any simple epithelium from a section by asking two questions in a fixed order — how many layers, then what shape are the cells at the free surface — and then use the shape to predict the job, so that squamous means exchange, cuboidal means absorption and secretion in a duct or tubule, and columnar means a busy absorptive or secretory surface. Then apply the two traps that make students misclassify: a tangential cut through a simple epithelium looks stratified, and pseudostratified epithelium looks stratified and is not.

structures.label: The two questions, asked in this order
structures.narration: Every epithelium in the body is named by the same two questions and the order matters. FIRST: how many layers of cells sit between the free surface and the basement membrane? One layer is simple; more than one is stratified. SECOND, and only then: what shape are the cells at the FREE SURFACE? Flat is squamous, as tall as wide is cuboidal, taller than wide is columnar. Asking shape first is the commonest way to get the answer wrong, because in a stratified epithelium the basal cells are a different shape from the surface cells and only the surface counts. Find the basement membrane, count up from it to the surface, then look at the top.

structures.label: The basement membrane — where counting starts
structures.narration: A thin sheet of extracellular matrix beneath every epithelium, and the line every count starts from. On a routine H&E it is often invisible and is inferred from where the cells stop; PAS stains it magenta and makes it explicit. It matters far beyond classification for two reasons. Epithelium is avascular — nothing crosses this sheet but diffusion, which is why an epithelium's thickness is limited by how far oxygen will travel. And it is the boundary that defines invasion: a malignant epithelial tumour that has not crossed it is carcinoma in situ, and the same tumour a millimetre later, through it, is invasive carcinoma with access to vessels and lymphatics.

structures.label: Polarity — three surfaces, three different memberships
structures.narration: An epithelial cell is not the same on all sides, and this single fact does more diagnostic work than any list. The APICAL surface faces the lumen or the outside world and carries whatever the cell does there — microvilli for absorption, cilia for movement. The LATERAL surfaces face the neighbours and carry the junctions that make the sheet a seal. The BASAL surface faces the basement membrane and anchors to it. Polarity is also visible at the lowest magnification through the nucleus: in a tall absorptive cell the nucleus sits basally, pushed down by the machinery above it, and a row of nuclei all at the same level near the base is one of the quickest confirmations that an epithelium is simple columnar rather than something else.

structures.label: Simple squamous — one flat layer, built for exchange
structures.narration: A single layer of flattened cells, so thin that at low power the only sign of it is a row of nuclei bulging into the space, each nucleus flattened with the cell. The shape is the function: where the barrier's job is to let things across, the barrier is made as thin as it can be. Hence the alveolus, where gas crosses in fractions of a micrometre; the glomerulus and the thin limb of the loop of Henle; and the linings that must be slippery rather than protective. Two of those linings have their own names and both are simple squamous: ENDOTHELIUM lines blood and lymphatic vessels, MESOTHELIUM lines the pleural, pericardial and peritoneal cavities. They are not different tissues, and knowing that is what makes mesothelioma a tumour of a serosal lining rather than a mystery.

structures.label: Simple cuboidal — one layer, as tall as it is wide
structures.narration: One layer of cells about as tall as they are wide, with a round central nucleus — the roundness and the central position are the fastest confirmation. This is the default epithelium of small ducts and tubules everywhere: the kidney tubules, the ducts of exocrine glands, the surface of the ovary, and the follicles of the thyroid where the cells surround stored colloid. It does moderate work in both directions, absorbing and secreting. On a kidney section it also teaches a distinction worth having early: the proximal convoluted tubule has a brush border of microvilli that blurs its lumen and stains deeply, while the distal tubule has a crisp clear lumen and more nuclei round it — same class of epithelium, different apical specialisation, and the specialisation is what tells them apart.

structures.label: Simple columnar — one layer, taller than wide
structures.narration: One layer of tall cells with oval nuclei lined up near the base. Height buys internal volume, so this is the epithelium of surfaces doing sustained absorptive or secretory work: the whole of the gut from stomach to rectum, the gallbladder, and — ciliated, with a different job — the uterine tube. Two apical specialisations decide which subtype you are looking at. Microvilli give the striated or brush border of the intestine, a fringe that multiplies surface area many times over. Cilia, longer and visibly separate, move the surface film, which is what the uterine tube uses to carry the oocyte. Goblet cells are scattered through it: single-celled mucous glands, pale and rounded because their mucin dissolves out in processing, and their number rises steadily from duodenum to colon. This is also the epithelium at the centre of Barrett's oesophagus, where acid reflux replaces the oesophagus's stratified squamous lining with an intestinal-type columnar one — metaplasia, a change of epithelial class, and a premalignant one.

structures.label: Pseudostratified — the one that lies about its layers
structures.narration: Every cell reaches the basement membrane; not every cell reaches the surface. The nuclei therefore sit at several different heights and the epithelium LOOKS stratified, but it is simple, and the definition — one layer, because all cells touch the basement membrane — is what the name is protesting about. Two places to know it. The airway, from nose to bronchi, is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells: mucus on top, cilia beating it mouthwards, the mucociliary escalator. Lose the cilia's function and you get the recurrent sinusitis and bronchiectasis of primary ciliary dyskinesia, with situs inversus in Kartagener's; poison them with cigarette smoke and the epithelium first loses cilia, then converts to stratified squamous altogether. The epididymis is the other, pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia — which are long microvilli, not cilia at all, and do not beat. That mis-naming is old and is not going to be fixed, so learn it as a name rather than as a fact.

structures.label: The tangential cut — the commonest reason for a wrong answer
structures.narration: A section is a two-dimensional slice through a three-dimensional sheet, and if the knife passes obliquely through a curved simple epithelium it cuts a long shallow ramp through one layer of cells and prints several rows of nuclei — a simple epithelium that reads as stratified. This is not a rare artefact; on any tubular organ some part of the wall is cut obliquely. Three checks settle it. Look for a region of the same section cut perpendicularly, where the epithelium suddenly becomes one clean layer. Follow the basement membrane: if it runs obliquely across the field rather than parallel to the surface, the cut is oblique. And ask whether the surface cells and the deep cells differ in kind, because a truly stratified epithelium changes character from base to surface while a tangentially cut simple one does not. The general rule is worth stating once for the whole course: never classify a tissue from the worst-cut part of the slide.

views.title: Two questions, in order
views.narration: Start at the basement membrane and count upwards, then look at the shape of the cells at the top. One layer is simple and the shape at the surface names it: squamous, cuboidal or columnar. That is the whole classification, and every difficulty in this topic is a difficulty in seeing one of those two things rather than in knowing the scheme. Nothing on this screen is a model: this is drawn artwork of a section, because what is being taught is arrangement at the cellular scale and no surface mesh has cells in it.

views.title: Polarity — why the nucleus tells you where you are
views.narration: Before the three types, one drawn cell with its three surfaces labelled: apical facing the lumen, lateral facing the neighbours, basal on the basement membrane. Two things follow that you will use on every slide. The apical specialisation — microvilli or cilia — tells you the job. And the position of the nucleus tells you the polarity at a magnification where you cannot yet see anything else: basally placed, evenly levelled nuclei mean a simple epithelium with tall cells, and nuclei at several heights mean either stratified or the pseudostratified impostor of beat 5.

views.title: The three simple types, side by side
views.narration: Three panels, one layer each, differing only in the height of the cell — and height is the variable that carries the meaning. Flat where the job is to let things across: alveolus, glomerulus, the lining of a vessel or a serous cavity. Cube-shaped where the job is moderate transport in a tube: kidney tubules, gland ducts, thyroid follicles. Tall where the job is sustained absorption or secretion and the cell needs volume to do it: stomach to rectum, gallbladder, uterine tube. Read left to right and the sequence is a graph of how much work the cell does against how thin the barrier can afford to be.

views.title: What sits on top — microvilli, cilia and goblet cells
views.narration: Same class, different apical surface, different organ. Microvilli, short and packed, give the intestinal brush border and multiply absorptive area; they are too small to resolve individually in the light microscope, which is why they appear as a stripe rather than as fringes. Cilia are longer, individually visible, and beat — the uterine tube and the airway use them to move a surface film. Goblet cells sit between the columnar cells as single-celled mucous glands, and their density rises from duodenum to colon. One diagnostic consequence to carry: a brush border in the kidney marks the proximal tubule and separates it from the distal at a glance, and goblet cells in an oesophageal biopsy are abnormal by definition and are the finding that makes it Barrett's.

views.title: Two ways a simple epithelium looks stratified
views.narration: Both panels show several rows of nuclei and neither is stratified, and the two are distinguished by different evidence. In PSEUDOSTRATIFIED epithelium the tissue really is like that: every cell reaches the basement membrane, only the tall ones reach the surface, and the nuclei sit at staggered heights everywhere you look. It is the airway lining and the epididymis, and it is a real, named, reproducible appearance. In a TANGENTIAL CUT the tissue is not like that at all and the microscope is lying: the plane of section ramped through a curved single layer. The distinguishing test is to move across the slide — the pseudostratified appearance persists wherever the epithelium is cut cleanly, the tangential one resolves into a single layer as soon as the cut becomes perpendicular. Follow the basement membrane to tell which you have.
